notes.meaning: Paul begins answering a question the Corinthians wrote to him about eating meat that had been offered to pagan idols. Some believers proudly claimed their superior knowledge gave them the right to eat whatever they wanted. Mere knowledge inflates people with self-importance, but Christian love acts to build others up in the faith.

Anyone who thinks he has mastered spiritual knowledge shows that he is still full of pride. True knowledge begins with humility before God and care for other people. If what we know does not lead us to love our neighbor, we have not truly understood it at all.

Loving God is far more important than possessing head knowledge that makes us proud. God recognizes and warmly accepts the person who truly loves Him. That love for God will always overflow into gentle care for our brothers and sisters.

Paul agrees with a basic truth about eating meat offered to idols: idols are not real gods. An idol is nothing more than a lifeless piece of wood or stone, with no real divine power. Christians know there is only one true God who created and rules the world.

Pagan people worshipped countless deities, from heavenly bodies like the sun and stars to earthly rulers and mythical heroes. People called these beings gods and bowed down to them as their masters. Paul points out that these beings are only called gods by humans, but they are not real gods in truth.

Christians confess only one God, the Father, who made all things and created us to live for His honor. We also confess only one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom the whole universe was made and through whom we have new life. Christ shares in the work of creation and divine rule as Lord alongside the Father.

Not all new believers in Corinth understood that idols have no real power. Some had spent their whole lives worshipping idols, so eating sacrificial meat still felt to them like worshipping a false god. Because their conscience—their inner sense of right and wrong—was still weak and poorly informed, doing something they felt was wrong left them feeling guilty and defiled.

Physical food does not bring us closer to God or win His special approval. We do not lose any spiritual standing before God if we choose not to eat, and we gain no extra points with Him if we do. God looks at the faith and love in our hearts rather than what sits on our dinner plates.

Believers must be very careful with their personal freedom in matters that are not sinful in themselves. A stumbling block is anything that trips someone up and leads them into sin. If our lawful choices cause a fellow believer with a tender conscience to fall, we have failed to act in love.

Pagan banquets were often held right inside idol temples in Corinth. If a struggling Christian sees a knowledgeable believer dining in a pagan temple, he may feel pushed to copy the behavior. Following that example while still believing the idol is real would lead that weaker believer straight into idolatry.

Boasting of our knowledge can bring terrible spiritual harm to a fellow Christian. Paul stresses how serious this is by reminding the strong that Christ died to rescue that very brother. We must never value our right to eat a meal above the spiritual well-being of someone Jesus gave His life to save.

differ.view: This warning proves that a genuine believer for whom Christ died can be led back into sin, lose faith, and perish eternally.
The verse warns about the ruinous tendency of such selfish behavior, but true believers are kept by God's power and will not finally be lost.

notes.meaning: Leading fellow Christians into actions that wound their conscience is a direct sin against them. Paul adds that it is also a sin against Christ Himself. Because Jesus is closely united with His people, mistreating a member of His body is the same as striking the Lord Himself.

Paul shows how love puts others first by offering his own life as an example. He declares that he would gladly give up eating meat forever rather than cause another Christian to stumble into sin. Christian freedom finds its greatest joy in laying aside personal rights to protect the faith of others.
